questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: The nurse is rounding on four clients who have indwelling urinary catheters. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client with a temperature of 38.8°C and new flank pain
A client whose drainage bag is clipped to the bed rail
A client who asks when the catheter will be removed
A client whose urine is cloudy with a strong odor
optionRationales: Correct. Fever and flank pain suggest a catheter-associated infection that may involve the kidney.
Incorrect. The bag needs to be repositioned, but this is a quick fix that does not reflect an active complication.
Incorrect. Early removal prevents infection and is worth addressing, but the question is not urgent.
Incorrect. Cloudy, odorous urine may signal infection and needs follow-up, but it lacks the systemic signs of the client with fever and flank pain.
questions.rationale: Urinary catheters are a leading source of health care-associated infections, because they give bacteria a direct path into the normally sterile bladder. Fever, flank pain, or cloudy, foul-smelling urine in a catheterized client suggests infection and should be reported. The client with fever and flank pain is showing systemic signs, so that client is seen first. The bag clipped to the bed rail is tempting because it is a real error that can cause backflow, but it is quickly corrected and has not yet caused harm.
questions.takeaway: Fever and flank pain in a client with a catheter suggest infection and come before routine catheter fixes.
questions.hintContent: Decide which client is showing signs that harm has already happened.
questions.hintStrategy: Actual problems with systemic signs come before potential problems the nurse can quickly correct.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse reviews new prescriptions for four clients. Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider before giving it?
options: Mirabegron for a client whose BP is 118/74
Oxybutynin for a client with glaucoma
Phenazopyridine for 2 days for a client with dysuria
Furosemide for a client whose potassium is 4.2 mEq/L
optionRationales: Incorrect. Mirabegron can raise BP, but this reading is normal; the nurse monitors BP.
Correct. Anticholinergics can raise pressure in the eye and are avoided in clients with glaucoma.
Incorrect. A short course for burning is the usual use of this urinary analgesic.
Incorrect. This potassium is normal, so the diuretic can be given with monitoring.
questions.rationale: Each urinary drug has a key caution. Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic, and the same blocking action that relaxes the bladder can raise pressure in the eye, which is why it is avoided in glaucoma. That makes it the prescription to question. Mirabegron is tempting because it can raise blood pressure, but this client's pressure is normal, so the nurse simply monitors. The other prescriptions fit their usual purpose and have safe pre-dose data.
questions.takeaway: Avoid oxybutynin (Ditropan) and other anticholinergics in clients with glaucoma.
questions.hintContent: Recall the key caution for each urinary drug class.
questions.hintStrategy: For clarify-the-order items, look for a drug paired with a condition or value that makes it unsafe.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 60-year-old client is started on mirabegron (Myrbetriq) for bladder spasms. Which assessment is most important for the nurse to monitor?
options: Urine color
Liver enzymes
Intraocular pressure
Blood pressure
optionRationales: Incorrect. Discolored urine is expected with phenazopyridine, not mirabegron.
Incorrect. Elevated liver and pancreatic enzymes are a caution for bethanechol.
Incorrect. Eye pressure is a concern with anticholinergics such as oxybutynin.
Correct. Mirabegron is a beta-3 agonist that can raise blood pressure, so BP is monitored.
questions.rationale: Mirabegron is a urinary antispasmodic that relaxes the detrusor by acting as a beta-3 agonist. It has significant side effects, and it can notably raise blood pressure, so the nurse monitors BP. Each distractor belongs to a different urinary drug, which is exactly how these items test you. Intraocular pressure is tempting because it is a caution for another bladder-calming drug, but that concern belongs to anticholinergics.
questions.takeaway: Mirabegron (Myrbetriq) can raise blood pressure; monitor BP.
questions.hintContent: Match the drug to its own key caution rather than one from a related drug.
questions.hintStrategy: When distractors are cautions for other drugs in the same family, sort each one to its own drug before choosing.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 77-year-old client newly prescribed hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) asks, "Does it matter when I take this?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Take it at bedtime so it can work while you are asleep."
"Take it whenever you remember, as long as it's daily."
"Take it with dinner so it is easier on your stomach."
"Take it in the morning so you are not up at night voiding."
optionRationales: Incorrect. A bedtime dose causes nocturia, broken sleep, and falls on the way to the bathroom.
Incorrect. Timing matters for a diuretic because of the increase in urine output.
Incorrect. An evening dose still causes increased voiding at night.
Correct. Morning dosing lets the diuretic effect happen during the day and reduces nighttime trips to the bathroom.
questions.rationale: Diuretics increase urine output for several hours after a dose. Giving them in the morning when possible keeps the client from being up all night voiding. For an older adult, nighttime trips to the bathroom also raise fall risk, so timing is a safety issue. The bedtime answer is tempting because many medications are taken then, but it turns a helpful drug into a cause of nocturia and falls.
questions.takeaway: Give diuretics in the morning to prevent nocturia and nighttime falls.
questions.hintContent: Think about when the increased urine output will occur after a dose.
questions.hintStrategy: For timing questions, picture the drug's effect happening at that time of day and judge the safety impact.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: On postoperative day 3, a 52-year-old client is walking in the hall independently and still has the indwelling urinary catheter placed for surgery. There is no current order addressing the catheter. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Change the catheter to a new one using sterile technique
Irrigate the catheter daily to keep it patent
Ask the provider whether the catheter is still needed
Remove the catheter now because the client is walking
optionRationales: Incorrect. Replacing the catheter keeps the infection risk going without a reason for a catheter.
Incorrect. Routine irrigation opens the closed system and increases infection risk.
Correct. The best prevention of catheter infection is removing the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed.
Incorrect. Removing a catheter requires an order; the nurse prompts the provider rather than acting alone.
questions.rationale: A catheter is a direct path for bacteria into the normally sterile bladder, and the longer it stays in, the higher the infection risk. The nurse should ask every day whether the catheter is still necessary and remind the provider when it may not be. This client is up and walking, so the original reason may no longer apply. Removing it immediately is tempting because it seems like the right outcome, but it requires an order, so the nurse advocates rather than acting outside scope.
questions.takeaway: Ask daily whether a catheter is still needed and prompt the provider to remove it when it is not.
questions.hintContent: Consider the single most effective way to prevent catheter-associated infection.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the action that achieves the safe outcome within the nurse's scope of practice.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A 75-year-old client recovering from a stroke is going home and has trouble getting on and off the toilet. The client will need grab bars, a raised toilet seat, and help with transfers. To which team member should the nurse request a referral?
options: Occupational therapist
Hospital social worker
Medical supply company
Home health aide service
optionRationales: Correct. The occupational therapist assesses toileting and transfer safety, teaches safe technique, and recommends grab bars and a raised toilet seat for the home.
Incorrect. A social worker can help arrange resources and coverage for equipment, but does not assess toileting function or teach safe transfers.
Incorrect. A supply company can deliver a raised seat and grab bars, but it does not assess the home or teach the client how to transfer safely.
Incorrect. An aide can physically help with transfers, but cannot assess needs or choose equipment; the therapist's plan should come first.
questions.rationale: Many clients leave the hospital still managing a urinary problem, so referrals before or after discharge are part of collaborative care. The occupational therapist helps the client toilet safely: transfers, adaptive clothing, raised toilet seats, and grab bars. The medical supply company is tempting because it provides equipment, but it does not assess the home or teach safe transfers. Matching the need to the right team member prevents falls and keeps the client independent.
questions.takeaway: Refer to occupational therapy for safe toileting, transfers, and bathroom equipment.
questions.hintContent: Match the client's specific needs to the team member whose role covers them.
questions.hintStrategy: For referral items, look for the team member whose role includes assessment and teaching, not just supplies.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 26-year-old client is taking phenazopyridine (Pyridium) and an antibiotic for a bladder infection. On day 2 the client calls and says, "The burning is gone, so I stopped the antibiotic. My urine is orange, though." Which part of the client's report should the nurse address first?
options: Having orange urine while taking phenazopyridine
Feeling less burning on the second day of treatment
Stopping the antibiotic because the burning has stopped
Planning to take the urinary analgesic for only 2 days
optionRationales: Incorrect. Orange or red urine is an expected effect of phenazopyridine.
Incorrect. Relief of burning is the intended effect of the urinary analgesic.
Correct. Phenazopyridine relieves pain but does not cure infection; the antibiotic must be taken for the full course.
Incorrect. Phenazopyridine is usually limited to about 2 days, so this is appropriate.
questions.rationale: Phenazopyridine is a urinary analgesic that treats pain and burning; it discolors the urine orange or red and is slightly sedating. Because it masks symptoms, a client may feel cured while the infection is still present. Antibiotics must be taken for the full course even when symptoms improve, so stopping early is the dangerous misunderstanding. The orange urine is tempting to address because the client mentions it with concern, but it is an expected and harmless effect.
questions.takeaway: Phenazopyridine masks pain but does not treat infection; the antibiotic must be finished.
questions.hintContent: Separate the drug that relieves symptoms from the drug that treats the cause.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client reports several things, address the one that could cause harm before the one that is expected.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a 41-year-old office worker with recurrent urinary tract infections about healthy bladder habits. Which statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: "I'll push hard with my pelvic muscles to empty faster."
"I'll spread my water intake out over the whole workday."
"I'll drink less water so I don't have to leave my desk."
"I'll go to the bathroom when I feel the urge instead of waiting."
"I'll cut back on the diet sodas with artificial sweetener."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Using the pelvic floor muscles to force urine out is a habit to avoid.
Correct. Adequate fluids dilute the urine and flush bacteria from the bladder.
Incorrect. Low intake concentrates urine, irritates the bladder, and raises infection risk.
Correct. Avoiding delayed voiding is a key healthy toileting habit.
Correct. Artificial sweeteners, caffeine, and alcohol are bladder irritants.
questions.rationale: Prevention teaching focuses on healthy weight and exercise, not delaying or straining to void, adequate fluids and fiber, avoiding bladder irritants such as caffeine, alcohol, and artificial sweeteners, and not smoking. Concentrated urine irritates the bladder wall, and urine that sits in the bladder gives bacteria time to grow. Drinking less to avoid trips to the bathroom is tempting for a busy worker, but it raises the very risk the client wants to lower. Straining is tempting because it seems to empty the bladder faster, but it stresses the pelvic floor.
questions.takeaway: Prevent urinary problems: void when the urge comes, drink enough, avoid irritants, and do not strain.
questions.hintContent: Recall the healthy toileting and intake habits that prevent urinary problems.
questions.hintStrategy: For teaching SATA, mark each statement as a healthy habit or a harmful one; do not let a convenient-sounding reason sway you.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: The nurse is recording intake for a client on strict intake and output. Which items should the nurse count as intake? Select all that apply.
options: One cup of ice chips
500 mL of IV normal saline
A serving of gelatin dessert
A slice of buttered toast
A bowl of mashed potatoes
Continuous tube feeding of 600 mL
optionRationales: Correct. Ice chips are liquid at room temperature and count as intake.
Correct. IV fluids are part of total intake.
Correct. Gelatin is liquid at room temperature and counts as intake.
Incorrect. Solid foods are not counted as fluid intake.
Incorrect. Mashed potatoes are not liquid at room temperature and are not counted.
Correct. Tube feedings are counted as intake.
questions.rationale: Intake and output are only useful if they are complete and accurate. All intake includes oral fluids, foods that are liquid at room temperature such as ice chips, gelatin, ice cream, and soup, IV fluids, and tube feedings. Solid foods are not counted even if they contain water. Mashed potatoes are tempting because they are soft, but they are not liquid at room temperature. Missing any source of intake can hide a dangerous imbalance.
questions.takeaway: Count oral fluids, anything liquid at room temperature, IV fluids, and tube feedings as intake.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each item would be a liquid if left on the counter.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply one clear rule to each option rather than judging by how watery a food seems.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 69-year-old client is prescribed IV furosemide (Lasix) for fluid overload. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Keep a urinal and the call light within the client's reach
Schedule the dose at bedtime to reduce daytime voiding
Teach the client to use a salt substitute at meals
Check potassium, sodium, BUN, and creatinine before giving
Weigh the client daily at the same time on the same scale
optionRationales: Correct. Increased urine output can lead to falls when clients rush to the bathroom.
Incorrect. Diuretics are given in the morning when possible to prevent nocturia.
Incorrect. Salt substitutes are a concern with potassium-sparing diuretics and are not part of furosemide teaching.
Correct. These labs are monitored with diuretics, and abnormal values are reported before the dose.
Correct. Daily weight shows whether fluid is coming off.
questions.rationale: Diuretics change fluid and electrolytes, so the nurse checks BUN, creatinine, potassium, and sodium before giving them, watches blood pressure, and tracks intake and output and daily weight. Increased urine output means the client will need to void often, so a urinal and call light within reach help prevent falls. Salt substitutes are tempting to recommend because they lower sodium, but they contain potassium and are a specific concern with spironolactone. Morning dosing keeps the client from voiding all night.
questions.takeaway: With diuretics: check labs first, weigh daily, prevent falls, and give the dose in the morning.
questions.hintContent: Think about what a strong diuretic does to electrolytes, fluid balance, and the number of trips to the bathroom.
questions.hintStrategy: In plan-of-care SATA, eliminate options that belong to a different drug in the same class.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 58-year-old client on hemodialysis has a new arteriovenous fistula in the right arm. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Auscultate the fistula for a bruit
Palpate the fistula for a thrill each shift
Start a peripheral IV in the right hand
Post a sign: no BP or blood draws in the right arm
Take blood pressure readings in the right arm
optionRationales: Correct. A bruit (whoosh) is the sound of blood flow through a working fistula.
Correct. A thrill (buzz) shows blood is flowing through the fistula.
Incorrect. The fistula arm is protected from needle sticks other than for dialysis.
Correct. Blood pressure cuffs and needle sticks can damage the fistula.
Incorrect. Compressing the fistula arm with a cuff can damage the access.
questions.rationale: Hemodialysis requires reliable access to the bloodstream, usually through a fistula or graft in the arm. The nurse protects it by avoiding blood pressure readings and blood draws in that arm and checks that it works by feeling a thrill and listening for a bruit. Starting an IV in the hand of the fistula arm is tempting because the hand is away from the fistula itself, but needle sticks in that arm can damage the access. Losing the fistula means losing the client's lifeline for dialysis.
questions.takeaway: Protect the fistula arm (no BP, blood draws, or IVs) and check it for a thrill and bruit.
questions.hintContent: Recall how the nurse confirms the fistula works and what can damage it.
questions.hintStrategy: For access-protection SATA, select actions that assess the access and reject anything that compresses or punctures that arm.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 71-year-old client with urinary retention has a new prescription for bethanechol (Urecholine). Which findings should the nurse report to the provider before giving the first dose? Select all that apply.
options: The client reports an urge to void but cannot
A urethral stricture that blocks urine flow
A history of asthma treated with an inhaler
Liver enzymes above the normal range
A heart rate of 48 beats/min
A post-void residual of 450 mL
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is the expected picture of retention that the drug is meant to treat.
Correct. A cholinergic is not used when something physically blocks urine flow.
Correct. Bethanechol can cause bronchoconstriction and should be avoided in asthma.
Correct. Bethanechol can elevate liver and pancreatic enzymes, so existing elevations are reported.
Correct. Bethanechol can slow the heart rate, so a low rate before the dose is reported.
Incorrect. A large residual is the reason the drug is being given.
questions.rationale: Bethanechol is a cholinergic that boosts the signal that makes the detrusor contract, so it promotes urination. It can elevate liver and pancreatic enzymes, and its cholinergic effects include sweating, salivation, flushing, cramping, a slow heart rate, and low blood pressure. It is avoided in asthma and is not used if something physically blocks urine flow, because a contracting bladder cannot push past a blockage. The large residual is tempting to report, but it is the indication for the drug, not a contraindication.
questions.takeaway: Before bethanechol, report asthma, an outflow obstruction, high liver enzymes, or a slow heart rate.
questions.hintContent: Think about what a drug that boosts the bladder's contraction signal does elsewhere in the body.
questions.hintStrategy: In pre-dose SATA, separate the indication for the drug from findings that make it unsafe.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: Four hours after a vaginal birth with an epidural, a 29-year-old client has not voided. Her fundus is firm, 2 cm above the umbilicus, and deviated to the right, and there is a soft bulge above the pubic bone. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Massage the fundus until it moves to midline
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter
Assist the client to the bathroom to void
Notify the provider of possible postpartum hemorrhage
optionRationales: Incorrect. The fundus is already firm; it is displaced by the bladder, which massage will not correct.
Incorrect. Catheterization is invasive and is used per protocol only if the client cannot void on her own.
Correct. A full bladder displaces the uterus and can increase bleeding, so emptying it with the least invasive method comes first.
Incorrect. The findings point to a distended bladder the nurse can address independently first.
questions.rationale: After birth, the bladder and urethra have been stretched and bruised, and an epidural may still dull sensation, so overdistention and incomplete emptying are common. Postpartum output also increases as the body sheds the extra fluid of pregnancy, so the bladder fills quickly. A full bladder pushes the uterus up and to one side and keeps it from contracting well, which can increase bleeding. Massaging the fundus is tempting because uterine position is abnormal, but this fundus is firm, and the cause of the displacement is the bladder. Helping her void comes first; a scan or catheter follows protocol only if she cannot.
questions.takeaway: A postpartum fundus displaced to one side with a suprapubic bulge means a full bladder: help the client void first.
questions.hintContent: Think about what pushes a firm uterus up and to the side after birth.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat the cause of the abnormal finding with the least invasive effective action.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse in a newborn nursery reviews the voiding records for four term infants. Which infant is the priority to report to the provider?
options: A 50-hour-old infant with no voids since birth
An 18-hour-old infant who has not yet voided
A 1-day-old infant whose urine looks cloudy
A 2-day-old infant who voids small amounts often
optionRationales: Correct. A newborn should void within 48 hours of delivery; no void by this age may signal a kidney or urinary tract problem.
Incorrect. Healthy newborns void within the first 24 hours, so this infant is still within the expected window.
Incorrect. Urine may be cloudy in the newborn and becomes straw-colored in early infancy.
Incorrect. Newborns void more frequently than older children because the bladder is small.
questions.rationale: Healthy newborns void within the first 24 hours, and it is important to make sure the newborn voids within 48 hours after delivery. If not, the provider needs to know, because this may signal a problem with the kidneys or urinary tract. Cloudy urine and frequent small voids are both expected in a newborn. The 18-hour-old is tempting because no void has occurred yet, but that infant is still inside the normal time frame.
questions.takeaway: Newborns void within 24 hours; no void by 48 hours is reported.
questions.hintContent: Recall the expected time of the first void and the outer limit before it becomes a concern.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each infant's age with the time benchmark; only the one past the limit needs a report.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A school nurse reviews four children whose parents have voiced concerns about wetting. Which child most needs a referral for further evaluation?
options: A 6-year-old deep sleeper who wets the bed a few nights a week
A 3-year-old who is dry all day but wets the bed most nights
A 4-year-old who has a daytime accident when very excited at play
A 9-year-old who was dry for years and now wets during the school day
optionRationales: Incorrect. Frequent bedwetting is worth discussing, but in a 6-year-old deep sleeper it is common and not considered a problem until after age 7.
Incorrect. Nighttime dryness develops after daytime control, so a 3-year-old who is dry by day but wet at night is developing normally.
Incorrect. Daytime wetting can be a concern, but urinary control develops through age 5, so an occasional accident during excited play at 4 is expected.
Correct. New daytime wetting after years of dryness in a school-age child may be pathologic, such as an infection, and needs evaluation.
questions.rationale: Most children develop urinary control between 2 and 5 years of age, and daytime control comes before nighttime control. Enuresis is common in school-age children, but the two types are interpreted differently. Bedwetting in deep sleepers is not a problem until after age 7, while daytime wetting may be pathologic and needs evaluation. The 6-year-old is tempting because the wetting happens several nights a week, but frequent bedwetting at that age in a deep sleeper still falls within normal.
questions.takeaway: Bedwetting is not a concern until after age 7; new daytime wetting may be pathologic and needs evaluation.
questions.hintContent: Separate nighttime wetting from daytime wetting and compare each child's age with the expected milestone.
questions.hintStrategy: In expected-versus-unexpected items, look for a change from the child's own baseline; regression is a red flag.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 90-year-old resident who usually chats at breakfast is drowsy and confused this morning. The nurse notes the findings in the exhibit. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Let the resident sleep this morning and reassess at lunchtime
Encourage a full glass of water now and recheck in an hour
Report the change in mental status and findings to the provider
Apply a bed alarm and document an increased risk for falls
optionRationales: Incorrect. Rest may seem kind, but new drowsiness and confusion are an acute change, and waiting until lunch delays care.
Incorrect. Fluids are part of the plan, but a drowsy resident may choke on a full glass, and new confusion can have other causes, such as infection, so the change must be reported.
Correct. New confusion with dark, concentrated urine and dry membranes suggests dehydration or another acute problem. The nurse offers fluids and reports the change so the cause can be evaluated.
Incorrect. A bed alarm addresses one consequence of the confusion, but it does nothing to identify or treat the cause.
questions.rationale: Older adults lose the ability to concentrate urine well, so they become dehydrated more easily, and signs of trouble may be subtle. New confusion, weakness, or a fall may be the first sign of dehydration or infection instead of thirst or burning. A full pitcher, dark amber urine, dry mucous membranes, and a specific gravity above 1.030 all support dehydration. The nurse offers fluids and reports the change in mental status. A bed alarm is tempting because the resident is confused, but it protects against one consequence without treating the cause.
questions.takeaway: In an older adult, new confusion may be the first sign of dehydration; report the change and address fluids.
questions.hintContent: Combine the intake, urine, and lab cues to identify the most likely cause of the confusion.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the action that addresses the cause and communicates a change in condition, rather than one that only manages a symptom.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: An 86-year-old client who takes HCTZ every morning gets up three times a night to void and has had two near-falls on the way to the bathroom. Which intervention is the priority?
options: Place a bedside commode and night-light, with the call light in reach
Restrict all fluids after 1200 to prevent voiding during the night
Ask the provider to move the morning HCTZ dose to bedtime instead
Teach the client to sit at the bed edge for a minute before standing
optionRationales: Correct. Shortening the trip, lighting the way, and keeping help in reach directly reduce the fall risk the client is already showing.
Incorrect. Tapering evening fluids is reasonable, but stopping all fluids at noon risks dehydration in an older adult.
Incorrect. Reviewing diuretic timing is reasonable, but a bedtime dose would increase nighttime voiding and falls.
Incorrect. Dangling before standing helps prevent orthostatic dizziness, but it does not shorten the walk to the bathroom or provide light and help, so it is incomplete.
questions.rationale: Aging kidneys excrete more fluid and electrolytes at night, so older adults often wake to void, and diuretics can make the problem worse. Nocturia is a safety issue because of falls on the way to the bathroom. A bedside commode, a night-light, a clear path, and a call light within reach reduce that risk right away. Restricting fluids is tempting because it seems to target the cause, but tapering fluids in the evening is appropriate, while cutting them off at noon risks dehydration.
questions.takeaway: For nocturia in an older adult, prevent falls with a commode, night-light, clear path, and call light.
questions.hintContent: Identify the most immediate physical risk created by this client's nighttime voiding.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client has had near-falls, safety interventions usually take priority over changes that take longer to work.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: An 88-year-old client is prescribed the standard adult dose of an antibiotic that is cleared by the kidneys. The client's creatinine clearance is 38 mL/min. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Contact the provider or pharmacist to review the dose
Give the dose as prescribed and monitor for side effects
Give the dose with extra fluids to help excretion
Hold the antibiotic until the next creatinine result
optionRationales: Correct. Reduced kidney function slows drug excretion, so a standard adult dose may build up to toxic levels.
Incorrect. Giving a dose that may be too high for the client's kidney function risks toxicity.
Incorrect. Fluids do not correct a dose that is too high for kidneys that clear drugs slowly.
Incorrect. Withholding treatment without a review delays care for the infection.
questions.rationale: Blood flow to the aging kidney decreases and GFR falls, so the kidneys clear wastes and drugs more slowly. That raises the risk of drug overdose and adverse effects, and doses often need to be lower. Normal creatinine clearance is 80 to 140 mL/min, so 38 mL/min shows significantly reduced function. Giving the dose and monitoring is tempting because the drug is prescribed, but the nurse is responsible for questioning a dose that the client's kidneys may not be able to clear.
questions.takeaway: Older adults clear kidney-excreted drugs more slowly; question standard adult doses when kidney function is low.
questions.hintContent: Compare the creatinine clearance with the normal range and think about what that means for drug excretion.
questions.hintStrategy: When a lab value suggests a dose may be unsafe, clarify before giving rather than giving and watching.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 2-day-old newborn receiving IV fluids for poor feeding is found with the infusion running at twice the prescribed rate. What should the nurse do first?
options: Weigh the newborn and compare with yesterday
Complete an incident report about the pump
Correct the pump to the prescribed rate
Count wet diapers over the past 8 hours
optionRationales: Incorrect. Weight helps assess the effect, but the excess infusion must be stopped first.
Incorrect. Reporting is required, but it comes after the infant is safe.
Correct. Stopping the excess fluid comes first, because newborn kidneys cannot get rid of extra water quickly.
Incorrect. Output data are useful, but they do not stop the ongoing excess fluid.
questions.rationale: A newborn's GFR is lower than an adult's, and newborns have limited ability to concentrate and dilute urine. They cannot get rid of extra water quickly, so a small IV error has a big effect, and monitoring for overhydration is essential. The first step is to stop the harm by correcting the rate; then the nurse assesses the infant, notifies the provider, and documents. Weighing the infant is tempting because it measures the problem, but measuring while the excess fluid keeps running delays the most important action.
questions.takeaway: Newborn kidneys cannot quickly excrete extra fluid; stop an IV error first, then assess and report.
questions.hintContent: Recall what limits a newborn's ability to handle extra fluid.
questions.hintStrategy: When harm is ongoing, the first action stops it; assessment and reporting follow.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The parent of a 6-year-old says, "He wets the bed a few nights a week, and he's impossible to wake up. He's dry all day." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "He should be evaluated for a urinary tract infection right away."
"Wake him every 2 hours during the night so he can use the toilet."
"Daytime and nighttime control should develop at the same time."
"Bedwetting is common in deep sleepers his age; limit drinks in the evening."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Bedwetting alone in a deep sleeper who is dry all day does not suggest infection.
Incorrect. Frequent waking disrupts sleep and is not the recommended first step for this age.
Incorrect. Daytime control normally comes before nighttime control.
Correct. Nocturnal enuresis is common in deep sleepers and not considered a problem until after age 7; limiting evening fluids and voiding before bed can help.
questions.rationale: Enuresis is common in school-age children, and nocturnal enuresis is especially prevalent in deep sleepers who do not wake to the signal of a full bladder. It is not considered a problem until after age 7, and most children outgrow it. The nurse reassures the parent and suggests limiting drinks in the evening and voiding before bed. Urging an infection workup is tempting because wetting can be a symptom, but daytime dryness and deep sleep point to normal development.
questions.takeaway: Bedwetting in a deep sleeper under age 7 is common; reassure and suggest evening fluid limits and voiding before bed.
questions.hintContent: Compare the child's age and pattern with the age at which bedwetting becomes a concern.
questions.hintStrategy: For parent-teaching items, the best answer is accurate, reassuring when appropriate, and gives a practical next step.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: On the first postpartum day, a 31-year-old client says, "I keep filling the hat with 500 to 700 mL every time I void. Is that normal?" The fundus is firm and midline. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: A sign of bladder overdistention that needs catheterization
An expected increase in output as the body sheds pregnancy fluid
Polyuria that suggests the client has new-onset diabetes
Retention with overflow of urine around a urethral blockage
optionRationales: Incorrect. Large voids with a firm, midline fundus show the bladder is emptying well.
Correct. Urinary output increases in the early postpartum period as the body gets rid of the extra fluid of pregnancy.
Incorrect. Postpartum diuresis is a normal physiologic change, not a sign of diabetes.
Incorrect. Overflow causes frequent small voids, not large, complete voids.
questions.rationale: Postpartum risks include overdistention, incomplete emptying, residual urine, and urinary tract infection, but urinary output also increases in the early postpartum period. Large voids and a firm, midline fundus show the bladder is filling quickly and emptying well. The nurse reassures the client and encourages her to void often because the bladder fills fast. Polyuria from diabetes is tempting because the volumes are large, but the timing and normal fundus point to expected diuresis.
questions.takeaway: Large voids on the first postpartum day are expected diuresis when the fundus is firm and midline.
questions.hintContent: Think about what happens to the extra fluid of pregnancy after birth.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the paired finding (a firm, midline fundus) to decide whether a striking value is expected or a problem.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: An 80-year-old client asks, "Why am I suddenly getting up at night to urinate when I never used to?" The client has no burning or leaking. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: "Your kidneys are making much less urine than they used to."
"As we age, the kidneys put out more fluid and electrolytes at night."
"Your bladder holds more urine now, so it fills up overnight."
"Older kidneys concentrate urine better, so you need to void more."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Less urine production would not explain more nighttime voiding.
Correct. Aging kidneys excrete more fluid and electrolytes at night, which causes nocturia.
Incorrect. The aging bladder becomes more fibrous and holds less, not more.
Incorrect. The aging kidney concentrates urine less well, not better.
questions.rationale: With aging, blood flow to the kidneys decreases, urine becomes more dilute, and the kidneys excrete more fluid and electrolytes at night. More urine at night interrupts sleep and can lead to falls on the way to the bathroom. The bladder also becomes more fibrous with decreased capacity. The option about a larger bladder is tempting because it seems to explain filling overnight, but capacity actually decreases with age.
questions.takeaway: Aging kidneys excrete more fluid at night, so nocturia is common in older adults.
questions.hintContent: Recall how the timing of kidney excretion changes with age.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each explanation for the direction of change; age-related items often reverse the true direction.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 79-year-old client who takes a thiazide diuretic for hypertension has a serum sodium of 128 mEq/L. Which explanation best accounts for this finding?
options: The client is retaining sodium because the kidneys filter less
A low-salt diet for high blood pressure has depleted the sodium
Older kidneys concentrate urine well, which pulls sodium out
Aging kidneys regulate sodium poorly, and the diuretic adds to the loss
optionRationales: Incorrect. GFR does fall with age, but sodium retention would raise the serum sodium, not lower it.
Incorrect. A low-salt diet is common with hypertension, but kidneys conserve sodium when intake falls, so diet alone rarely drops sodium this low.
Incorrect. Aging kidneys concentrate urine less well, not better, so this does not explain the finding.
Correct. Aging kidneys have trouble regulating sodium and water, and the thiazide adds to the loss; together they best explain a sodium of 128 mEq/L.
questions.rationale: Aging kidneys have trouble regulating sodium and water, which raises the risk of hyponatremia, a low blood sodium. Prescription diuretics, often taken for high blood pressure, add to the kidneys' trouble regulating electrolytes. The combination explains a sodium of 128 mEq/L in this client. Sodium retention from a lower GFR is tempting because GFR does fall with age, but retention would push sodium up rather than down.
questions.takeaway: Older adults on diuretics are at high risk for hyponatremia.
questions.hintContent: Combine two factors: age-related changes in sodium handling and the effect of the medication.
questions.hintStrategy: For explanation items, choose the option that accounts for every cue in the stem, including the medication.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: An 83-year-old woman at a clinic visit says, "I leak a little urine every day, but that's just part of getting old." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Leaking is not a normal part of aging; let's look for a treatable cause."
"You're right; most women your age leak, so pads are the best option."
"Drinking less water during the day should stop most of the leaking."
"Kegel exercises usually fix this, so start doing them every day."
optionRationales: Correct. Incontinence is never a normal part of aging. Correcting the belief and seeking a cause, such as infection, medication, or constipation, comes before choosing a treatment.
Incorrect. Pads can protect skin and feel supportive, but agreeing that leaking is normal leaves a treatable problem unexamined.
Incorrect. Some clients limit fluids to control leaking, but less water concentrates urine, irritates the bladder, and risks dehydration.
Incorrect. Pelvic floor exercises help many women with stress incontinence, but the cause has not been evaluated yet, so recommending a treatment is premature.
questions.rationale: Even with the age-related changes of a smaller, stiffer bladder and weaker pelvic floor, incontinence and retention are never a normal part of aging. They often indicate another medical problem, such as an infection, a medication effect, or constipation. The nurse corrects the belief kindly and encourages evaluation. Agreeing and suggesting pads is tempting because it feels supportive, but it leaves a treatable problem unexamined.
questions.takeaway: Incontinence is never a normal part of aging; encourage evaluation for a cause.
questions.hintContent: Recall whether incontinence is ever considered normal, at any age.
questions.hintStrategy: For therapeutic communication, choose the response that is accurate and moves the client toward care, not one that simply agrees.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The parent of a 1-day-old infant is worried because the baby's urine looks cloudy in the diaper. The infant is feeding well and has voided twice. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: Abnormal; cloudy urine suggests a urinary tract infection
Expected; newborn urine may be cloudy and becomes straw-colored
Abnormal; the infant is dehydrated and needs more fluid
Abnormal; cloudy urine shows the kidneys are not filtering yet
optionRationales: Incorrect. In a newborn who is feeding and voiding well, cloudy urine alone is expected.
Correct. Urine may be cloudy in the newborn and becomes straw-colored in early infancy.
Incorrect. Voiding twice in the first day and feeding well do not suggest dehydration.
Incorrect. The kidneys are working, since the infant has voided twice; cloudy urine is an expected newborn finding.
questions.rationale: Newborn kidneys are immature, with a lower GFR and limited ability to concentrate and dilute urine. Urine may be cloudy in the newborn and becomes straw-colored in early infancy. This infant is feeding well and voiding, so the cloudy urine is an expected finding. Interpreting it as infection is tempting because cloudy urine suggests infection in adults, but normal findings differ by age.
questions.takeaway: Cloudy urine can be normal in a newborn; it becomes straw-colored in early infancy.
questions.hintContent: Think about how newborn urine differs from adult urine.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether a finding that is abnormal in adults might be normal for this age group.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care to promote urinary health for an 85-year-old resident in long-term care. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the pharmacist to review doses of kidney-cleared drugs
Monitor sodium, BUN, and creatinine and report changes
Encourage fluids during the day and taper them in the evening
Schedule the resident's diuretic for bedtime
Limit fluids to 1,000 mL per day to reduce incontinence
Offer the toilet every 2 to 3 hours while awake
optionRationales: Correct. Aging kidneys excrete drugs more slowly, so doses may need to be lower.
Correct. Older adults are at risk for hyponatremia and reduced kidney function.
Correct. This prevents dehydration while reducing nocturia.
Incorrect. Diuretics are best taken in the morning to prevent nocturia.
Incorrect. Restricting fluids raises the risk of dehydration in a client who already loses water easily.
Correct. Scheduled toileting helps a smaller bladder empty before the urge becomes urgent.
questions.rationale: Because older adults lose water easily, clear drugs slowly, and void more at night, care focuses on hydration, medication safety, sleep, and fall prevention. The nurse encourages fluids during the day and tapers them in the evening, offers the toilet on a schedule, reviews medications, and monitors labs. Restricting fluids to 1,000 mL is tempting because it seems to reduce leaking, but it increases dehydration and concentrated, irritating urine.
questions.takeaway: Older adult urinary care: daytime fluids, scheduled toileting, medication review, lab monitoring, and morning diuretics.
questions.hintContent: Link each intervention to an age-related kidney or bladder change.
questions.hintStrategy: For plan-of-care SATA, reject options that trade one problem (incontinence) for a more dangerous one (dehydration).

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: Six hours after giving birth, a 33-year-old client says she voided but still feels full. Which findings suggest bladder distention? Select all that apply.
options: Lochia heavier than it was an hour ago
Frequent voids of 50 to 75 mL each
Fundus above the umbilicus and deviated to the right
Firm fundus at the umbilicus in the midline
A soft, rounded bulge above the symphysis pubis
optionRationales: Correct. A full bladder keeps the uterus from contracting well, which can increase bleeding.
Correct. Small, frequent voids suggest incomplete emptying with residual urine.
Correct. A full bladder pushes the uterus up and to the side.
Incorrect. A firm, midline fundus is the expected position when the bladder is not distended.
Correct. A suprapubic bulge suggests a distended bladder.
questions.rationale: Postpartum risks include overdistention of the bladder, incomplete emptying, and residual urine. A distended bladder displaces the uterus upward and to one side, produces a bulge above the pubic bone, and keeps the uterus from contracting, which can increase bleeding. Frequent small voids suggest the bladder is not emptying completely. A firm, midline fundus is tempting to include because the fundus is part of the assessment, but that position is what the nurse expects when the bladder is empty.
questions.takeaway: Postpartum bladder distention: displaced fundus, suprapubic bulge, small frequent voids, and heavier bleeding.
questions.hintContent: Think about how a full bladder affects the position and tone of the uterus.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA, the one option describing a normal finding is often the distractor among several related abnormal findings.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A breastfed newborn is 30 hours old and has had no wet diapers. Which assessments should the nurse perform? Select all that apply.
options: Hold feedings until the infant voids
Gentle palpation for bladder distention
Specific gravity of a catheterized specimen
Signs that the infant is in pain
Observation for restlessness
How often and how well the infant is feeding
optionRationales: Incorrect. Holding feedings reduces intake and could cause dehydration; intake is assessed, not stopped.
Correct. A distended bladder suggests urine is being made but not passed.
Incorrect. The nurse does not catheterize a newborn to obtain this; bedside assessment and reporting come first.
Correct. Pain is part of the assessment when a newborn has not voided.
Correct. Restlessness can signal discomfort from a full bladder or another problem.
Correct. Fluid intake is assessed when a newborn has not voided.
questions.rationale: Healthy newborns void within the first 24 hours, and it is important to make sure they void within 48 hours. If a newborn has not voided, the nurse assesses fluid intake, bladder distention, restlessness, and pain, documents carefully, and reports to the provider. Holding feedings is clearly harmful, and a catheterized specimen is tempting because it seems thorough, but it is invasive and not part of the nurse's initial assessment.
questions.takeaway: No newborn void: assess intake, bladder distention, restlessness, and pain, then report.
questions.hintContent: Recall the four areas to assess when a newborn has not voided.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose noninvasive bedside assessments over invasive procedures that need an order.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 27-year-old client is in her first trimester. Which urinary changes should the nurse teach her to expect during the pregnancy? Select all that apply.
options: Frequency that eases in the second trimester
Frequency that returns in the third trimester
Frequency now, because the uterus is pressing on the bladder
Burning with voiding as a normal part of pregnancy
A gradual fall in kidney filtration as birth nears
optionRationales: Correct. Frequency decreases as the uterus rises out of the pelvis.
Correct. The baby drops into the pelvis and presses on the bladder again.
Correct. Early in pregnancy the growing uterus sits against the bladder.
Incorrect. Dysuria suggests infection and should be reported.
Incorrect. GFR rises early in pregnancy and stays high until birth.
questions.rationale: The enlarging uterus presses against the bladder, increasing urinary frequency in the first trimester. Frequency decreases in the second trimester when the uterus rises into the abdomen and reappears in the third trimester when the baby settles onto the bladder. GFR rises early, reaching as much as 50% above normal by the second trimester, and stays high until birth. Burning is tempting to include because pregnancy causes so many urinary changes, but dysuria points to infection.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy frequency follows a pattern: first trimester, eases in the second, returns in the third.
questions.hintContent: Picture where the uterus sits in each trimester.
questions.hintStrategy: For expected-change SATA, reject options that describe a sign of illness or reverse the true direction of change.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: An 84-year-old client develops toxicity from a usual adult dose of a kidney-cleared medication. Which age-related changes help explain this? Select all that apply.
options: A lower glomerular filtration rate
Increased bladder capacity with aging
An improved ability to concentrate urine
Decreased blood flow to the kidneys
Impaired excretion of drugs by the kidneys
optionRationales: Correct. GFR diminishes with age, so drugs are cleared more slowly.
Incorrect. The aging bladder holds less, and bladder size does not affect drug clearance.
Incorrect. Aging kidneys concentrate urine less well.
Correct. The vessels supplying the kidneys atrophy, so less blood is filtered.
Correct. Slower excretion lets the drug build up to toxic levels.
questions.rationale: Blood flow to the kidneys decreases with age because the supplying vessels shrink, which lowers GFR. As a result, the kidneys clear wastes and drugs more slowly, increasing the risk of overdose and adverse effects. Doses often need to be lower in older adults. Increased bladder capacity is tempting because it sounds like a structural change, but bladder capacity actually decreases and has no role in drug excretion.
questions.takeaway: Lower renal blood flow and GFR in older adults slow drug excretion and raise toxicity risk.
questions.hintContent: Trace a drug's path out of the body through the kidneys and what aging changes along the way.
questions.hintStrategy: Select only changes that affect filtration and excretion; bladder changes are a common distractor.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an 87-year-old resident at risk for a urinary tract infection. Which findings could be early signs of infection in this resident? Select all that apply.
options: Waking once each night to void, as usual
A slightly smaller bladder capacity on exam
A fall while walking to the dining room
New weakness with difficulty standing
New confusion that was not present yesterday
optionRationales: Incorrect. A stable pattern of nocturia is common with aging.
Incorrect. Decreased capacity is an expected age-related change.
Correct. A fall can be an atypical sign of infection or dehydration in older adults.
Correct. Weakness may appear instead of the classic signs of infection.
Correct. In older adults, confusion may be the first sign of a urinary tract infection.
questions.rationale: Signs of trouble may be subtle in older adults. A resident with dehydration or a urinary tract infection may show new confusion, weakness, or a fall instead of thirst, burning, or fever. Recognizing these atypical signs leads to earlier assessment, a urinalysis and culture, and treatment. Usual nocturia is tempting to select because it involves voiding, but it is the resident's baseline and an expected age-related change.
questions.takeaway: Older adults with a urinary tract infection may present with new confusion, weakness, or a fall.
questions.hintContent: Think about how infection often presents differently in older adults.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for a change from baseline; stable, expected age-related findings are not early warning signs.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: Two days after abdominal surgery, a 63-year-old client has a distended, firm abdomen, is nauseated, and has not passed flatus. The nurse hears no bowel sounds after listening carefully. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the prescribed oral stimulant laxative
Offer clear liquids to stimulate peristalsis
Encourage ambulation and reassess tomorrow
Withhold oral intake and notify the provider
optionRationales: Incorrect. A laxative cannot move contents through a bowel that has stopped moving and may increase distress.
Incorrect. Fluids by mouth add to the contents that cannot move forward and can increase vomiting.
Incorrect. Walking helps peristalsis, but waiting until tomorrow delays reporting a possible obstruction.
Correct. These findings suggest a paralytic ileus; keeping the client NPO and reporting promptly prevents worsening distention and vomiting.
questions.rationale: A paralytic ileus is a functional obstruction in which the intestinal muscles stop moving, often after surgery or drugs such as anesthesia and opioids. Fluid, gas, and stool build up, the bowel stretches, and pressure can cut off blood flow, leading to necrosis and perforation. Distention, nausea, no flatus, and absent bowel sounds call for keeping the client NPO as ordered and reporting promptly; a nasogastric tube is often ordered. Ambulation is tempting because it does promote peristalsis, but it does not replace prompt reporting of a likely obstruction.
questions.takeaway: Post-op distention, no flatus, and absent bowel sounds suggest paralytic ileus: keep NPO and notify the provider.
questions.hintContent: Identify which type of obstruction is likely after surgery and what adding anything by mouth would do.
questions.hintStrategy: When the bowel has stopped moving, eliminate any option that puts more into the gut.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: An 82-year-old client has had six watery stools since morning, reports dizziness when standing, and has voided only 150 mL in 8 hours. Which problem should the nurse address as the priority?
options: Risk for perianal skin breakdown
Fluid and electrolyte loss
Risk for falls when standing
Risk for spreading infection
optionRationales: Incorrect. Skin breakdown is a real risk with diarrhea, but it is a potential problem and not life-threatening right now.
Correct. Dizziness on standing and only 150 mL of urine in 8 hours show an actual fluid deficit that is already affecting circulation in an older adult.
Incorrect. Fall risk matters with orthostatic dizziness, but the dizziness is caused by fluid loss; correcting circulation addresses the root problem.
Incorrect. Infection control matters if the diarrhea is infectious, but it is a potential problem and less urgent than the client's actual fluid loss.
questions.rationale: Diarrhea is the passage of liquid feces with increased frequency, and it brings two big nursing risks: fluid and electrolyte loss and skin breakdown. Water, sodium, and potassium leave with the stool, and infants and older adults become dehydrated fastest. Dizziness on standing and low urine output show the loss is already affecting circulation. Skin breakdown is tempting because it is a known risk of diarrhea, but it is not life-threatening right now.
questions.takeaway: With diarrhea, fluid and electrolyte loss comes before skin care, especially in older adults.
questions.hintContent: Look for cues showing the diarrhea is already affecting circulation.
questions.hintStrategy: Use Maslow and ABCs: a physiologic threat to circulation outranks skin and psychosocial needs.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with a mechanical bowel obstruction from adhesions has a nasogastric tube to suction. Which finding indicates the client's condition is worsening?
options: The client passes a small amount of flatus for the first time
Nasogastric drainage decreases from 400 to 150 mL per shift
The client reports less cramping and passes a soft stool
The abdomen becomes rigid, temperature is 38.9°C, and HR is 124
optionRationales: Incorrect. Passing flatus suggests contents are starting to move past the obstruction.
Incorrect. Less drainage suggests less fluid backing up behind the blockage.
Incorrect. Less cramping with passage of stool shows contents are moving again, a sign of improvement.
Correct. Rigidity with fever and tachycardia suggests bowel necrosis or perforation, the key risks of obstruction.
questions.rationale: In a bowel obstruction, contents stop moving, the bowel stretches, and pressure inside it squeezes its own blood vessels. Without blood, bowel tissue dies and can tear open, spilling contents into the abdomen. A rigid abdomen with fever and a rapid heart rate suggests necrosis or perforation and needs immediate reporting. Decreasing NG drainage is tempting to read as a warning that the tube is not working, but with passing flatus and stool it reflects less fluid backing up behind the blockage.
questions.takeaway: Rigid abdomen, fever, and tachycardia in bowel obstruction suggest necrosis or perforation.
questions.hintContent: Recall what happens to the bowel wall when pressure behind an obstruction cuts off its blood supply.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluate-outcome items, decide whether each option shows improvement or deterioration before choosing.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 89-year-old resident who has not had a formed bowel movement in 6 days is now passing small amounts of liquid stool several times a day. The AP reports this and asks whether the resident needs the PRN antidiarrheal. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give the PRN antidiarrheal to slow the stools
Assess the resident for a fecal impaction
Increase the resident's fluids to replace losses
Obtain a stool specimen to test for infection
optionRationales: Incorrect. Slowing the bowel would make an impaction worse.
Correct. Liquid stool seeping after days without a formed stool suggests an impaction, and an antidiarrheal would worsen it.
Incorrect. Fluids are helpful but do not address the likely blockage of hard stool.
Incorrect. Testing for infection skips the more likely cause suggested by the history.
questions.rationale: Constipation that goes untreated can build into a fecal impaction. A client with an impaction may pass small amounts of liquid stool that seeps around the hard mass, which looks like diarrhea even though the real problem is a blockage. Six days without a formed stool followed by liquid leakage fits that pattern. Giving the antidiarrheal is tempting because the stool is liquid, but it would slow the bowel further and worsen the impaction. The nurse assesses before acting.
questions.takeaway: Liquid stool after days without a formed stool suggests impaction; assess before giving an antidiarrheal.
questions.hintContent: Think about what can cause liquid stool in a client who has not had a formed stool for days.
questions.hintStrategy: When a request seems routine, check whether the history points to a different problem that the requested drug would worsen.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse is delegating care of a 76-year-old client who has frequent liquid stools and a strong urge that is hard to control. Which instruction to the assistive personnel (AP) is the priority?
options: Record the number of stools on the flow sheet each shift
Encourage the client to delay toileting until a set time
Keep the commode at the bedside and answer the call light at once
Put an incontinence brief on the client to protect the bed linens
optionRationales: Incorrect. Accurate stool counts are useful data, but physical safety comes first when the client has an urgent need to toilet.
Incorrect. Scheduled toileting helps some continence problems, but diarrhea makes the urge hard to control, so delaying risks accidents.
Correct. With diarrhea the urge is hard to control, so a commode in reach and a prompt response prevent falls and incontinence episodes.
Incorrect. A brief may seem practical, but it traps liquid stool against the skin, raises the risk of breakdown, and does not help the client reach the toilet.
questions.rationale: With diarrhea, the urge to defecate is difficult or impossible to control, so clients may not make it to the bathroom. Keeping the call light, bedpan, or commode within reach and answering quickly prevents both falls and incontinence episodes. Recording stools is tempting because accurate data matter, but physical safety comes first. Asking the client to hold stool until a scheduled time ignores how diarrhea affects control.
questions.takeaway: For clients with diarrhea, keep toileting equipment within reach and answer calls quickly.
questions.hintContent: Think about what diarrhea does to the client's ability to wait.
questions.hintStrategy: When delegating, the priority instruction usually prevents the most immediate physical harm.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client on postoperative opioids with no bowel movement for 2 days
A client with diverticulosis found on routine colonoscopy
A client whose inguinal hernia is now firm and painful, with vomiting
A client who has a bowel movement every day but strains to pass it
optionRationales: Incorrect. Constipation risk is expected with opioids and needs a plan, but it is not an emergency.
Incorrect. Diverticulosis is often symptom-free and is not an acute problem.
Correct. A trapped loop of bowel in a hernia can cause a mechanical obstruction and lose its blood supply.
Incorrect. This describes constipation that needs teaching, not urgent assessment.
questions.rationale: Hernias are a mechanical cause of bowel obstruction: a loop of bowel becomes trapped in a weak spot. A hernia that becomes firm and painful with vomiting suggests the bowel is trapped and may lose blood flow, leading to necrosis and perforation. That makes it the priority. The postoperative client on opioids is tempting because two days without a stool sounds concerning, but slowed bowel function is an expected effect that can be managed.
questions.takeaway: A hernia that becomes firm and painful with vomiting suggests mechanical obstruction and needs immediate assessment.
questions.hintContent: Identify the client whose bowel may be losing its blood supply.
questions.hintStrategy: Acute and unstable comes before chronic or expected; look for the client with new, worsening symptoms.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: On the first day after a hysterectomy, a 48-year-old client reports bloating and cramping from gas. Bowel sounds are present but hypoactive. Which nursing intervention is best?
options: Offer a carbonated drink to relieve the bloating
Encourage the client to drink through a straw
Help the client walk in the hallway as allowed
Keep the client on bed rest until the gas passes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Carbonated drinks add swallowed air and gas.
Incorrect. Drinking through a straw adds swallowed air.
Correct. Movement stimulates peristalsis and helps move gas along after abdominal surgery.
Incorrect. Immobility slows peristalsis and makes gas build up.
questions.rationale: Flatulence is excessive gas in the intestines or colon, and abdominal surgery is one cause because peristalsis slows afterward. Activity stimulates peristalsis, so walking as allowed helps move the gas along. Carbonated drinks and straws are tempting comfort measures, but both add swallowed air, which is another cause of gas. Bed rest seems restful but slows the bowel further.
questions.takeaway: After abdominal surgery, walking as allowed helps relieve gas by stimulating peristalsis.
questions.hintContent: Think about what stimulates peristalsis and what adds swallowed air.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that add to the cause of the problem, then choose the one that restores normal function.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 59-year-old client on bed rest who is taking oxycodone reports hard, dry stools that are difficult to pass. Which explanation best accounts for the change in stool?
options: The small intestine stops absorbing nutrients from food
Slower movement gives the colon more time to absorb water
Faster movement prevents water from being absorbed
The colon secretes extra fluid into the stool as it passes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Nutrient absorption is not the reason stool becomes hard.
Correct. Opioids and immobility decrease motility, so stool stays longer in the colon and loses more water.
Incorrect. Faster movement causes liquid stool, not hard stool.
Incorrect. Extra fluid would soften stool, not harden it.
questions.rationale: The colon's main job is to absorb water and electrolytes and store waste. The longer stool sits in the colon, the more water is removed and the harder it gets. Opioids and immobility both slow peristalsis, which gives the colon extra time to pull water from the stool. The option about faster movement is tempting if you mix up the directions, but rapid movement causes diarrhea because there is no time to absorb water.
questions.takeaway: Slow motility means more water absorbed and harder stool; fast motility means liquid stool.
questions.hintContent: Think of the colon as a sponge and consider how time affects how much water it absorbs.
questions.hintStrategy: For pathophysiology items, predict the mechanism yourself before reading the options, then match it.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A routine colonoscopy shows diverticula in a 62-year-old client who has no symptoms. The client asks, "Does this mean I have diverticulitis?" Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: "Having the pouches without inflammation is called diverticulosis."
"Yes, any pouches in the colon wall are called diverticulitis."
"Yes, and you will need surgery soon to remove all of the pouches."
"No, the pouches are simply a normal part of the colon lining."
optionRationales: Correct. Diverticulosis means the outpouchings are present, often without symptoms; diverticulitis means they are inflamed.
Incorrect. Diverticulitis refers to inflamed diverticula, not their simple presence.
Incorrect. Many people have diverticulosis without symptoms, and surgery is not routine.
Incorrect. Diverticula are herniations through weak spots in the wall, not a normal structure.
questions.rationale: Diverticula form when the mucosal lining herniates through weak spots in the bowel wall. Simply having these pouches is diverticulosis, and many people have them without symptoms. Diverticulitis means the pouches are inflamed, which can lead to obstruction, perforation, and bleeding. The option calling the pouches normal is tempting because the client has no symptoms, but they are an abnormal finding. The nurse can also teach the client to report lower left abdominal pain, fever, or changes in bowel habits.
questions.takeaway: Diverticulosis = pouches present; diverticulitis = pouches inflamed.
questions.hintContent: Separate the presence of the pouches from inflammation of the pouches.
questions.hintStrategy: For look-alike terms, focus on the suffix: -osis is a condition, -itis is inflammation.
