questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing two clients with abdominal distention and no passage of stool. Which finding best helps distinguish an early mechanical obstruction from a paralytic ileus?
options: High-pitched bowel sounds rather than absent bowel sounds
Nausea and vomiting rather than a lack of appetite
Abdominal distention rather than a flat, soft abdomen
No passage of flatus rather than frequent passage of flatus
optionRationales: Correct. With a mechanical blockage, bowel sounds are often high-pitched early; with an ileus they are hypoactive or absent.
Incorrect. Nausea and vomiting occur with both types of obstruction.
Incorrect. Distention occurs in both types because contents build up.
Incorrect. Both types stop the passage of stool and flatus.
questions.rationale: A mechanical obstruction is a physical block; the bowel muscle may still be working hard, so bowel sounds are often high-pitched early. A functional obstruction such as paralytic ileus means peristalsis has stopped, so bowel sounds are hypoactive or absent. Distention, cramping, vomiting, and no stool or flatus occur in both. Distention is tempting because it is so prominent, but a finding shared by both conditions cannot tell them apart.
questions.takeaway: Early mechanical obstruction: high-pitched bowel sounds; paralytic ileus: hypoactive or absent bowel sounds.
questions.hintContent: Think about whether the bowel muscle is still working in each type of obstruction.
questions.hintStrategy: To distinguish two conditions, eliminate every finding they share; the answer is the one that differs.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: Three weeks after a vaginal birth with a perineal tear, a 30-year-old client reports going 5 days between bowel movements and says, "I hold it because it hurts." Which factor best explains her constipation?
options: Pregnancy hormones that are still slowing the bowel
Medications that speed up peristalsis
Stress that increases bowel movement
Pain that leads her to delay defecation
optionRationales: Incorrect. The hormonal slowing of pregnancy fades after birth, and her own words point to a different cause.
Incorrect. Faster peristalsis would cause looser stools, not constipation.
Incorrect. Stress can speed the bowel up; it would not cause hard, infrequent stool.
Correct. Pain from a perineal tear makes a person delay defecation, and stool that sits longer becomes harder.
questions.rationale: Pain is one of the factors that affect bowel elimination: hemorrhoids, an incision, or a perineal tear make a person delay defecation. Ignoring the urge lets stool dry out and harden, which makes the next bowel movement even more painful. This client tells the nurse exactly that. The stress option is tempting because new parents are often stressed, but stress tends to speed the bowel up rather than slow it.
questions.takeaway: Pain from hemorrhoids, incisions, or perineal tears leads clients to delay defecation and become constipated.
questions.hintContent: Use the client's own words to identify which bowel factor is at work.
questions.hintStrategy: When the client states the reason, choose the option that matches it rather than an unrelated risk.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 34-year-old client reports leaking stool and gas since a difficult birth with a severe tear 3 months ago. Which cause of fecal incontinence is most likely?
options: A neurologic disorder such as dementia
Depression reducing her response to the urge
Inflammation from diverticulitis
Traumatic injury to the anal sphincter
optionRationales: Incorrect. Nothing in the stem suggests a neurologic disease.
Incorrect. Depression can contribute, but the history points to a physical injury.
Incorrect. No signs of inflammation are described, and the timing links to the birth.
Correct. Damage to the sphincter during childbirth is a traumatic cause of fecal incontinence.
questions.rationale: Fecal incontinence is the inability to voluntarily control the passage of feces and gas through the anal sphincter. It is usually a manifestation of another disorder. Controlling the bowel takes sensation, a strong sphincter, and a brain that can respond. Traumatic injury such as sphincter damage during childbirth is one listed cause and fits this history. Depression is tempting because it is common after birth, but the timing and the tear point directly to sphincter injury.
questions.takeaway: Fecal incontinence is usually a sign of another problem; sphincter injury during childbirth is a traumatic cause.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three things needed for bowel control and which one a severe tear damages.
questions.hintStrategy: Link the timing of the symptom to the event in the history.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 20-year-old college student reports cramping and loose stools during final exams that resolve after exams end. Which factor best explains this pattern?
options: Depression slowing down the bowel
Psychologic stress speeding up the bowel
Swallowed air from eating meals too quickly
Anesthesia slowing peristalsis in the colon
optionRationales: Incorrect. Depression tends to slow the bowel, causing constipation.
Correct. Stress can speed the bowel up, leaving less time to absorb water.
Incorrect. Swallowed air causes gas and bloating rather than loose stools.
Incorrect. No surgery or anesthesia is described.
questions.rationale: Psychologic factors affect how fast the bowel runs: stress can speed it up, and depression can slow it down. When contents rush through the colon too fast to absorb water, stool becomes loose. The pattern of symptoms during exams that resolve afterward points to stress. Depression is tempting because it is also a psychologic factor, but it moves the bowel in the opposite direction.
questions.takeaway: Stress can speed the bowel and cause loose stools; depression can slow it.
questions.hintContent: Match the direction of the bowel change to the psychologic factor.
questions.hintStrategy: When two options name related factors, check which direction each one pushes the bowel.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 74-year-old client is on bed rest after a hip fracture. Which factors in the client's record increase the risk for constipation? Select all that apply.
options: Fluid intake of about 800 mL per day
Ferrous sulfate (iron) twice daily
Bed rest with limited movement
A broad-spectrum IV antibiotic
A high-fiber breakfast cereal each day
Morphine every 4 hours for pain
optionRationales: Correct. Too little fluid means harder, drier stool.
Correct. Iron supplements constipate.
Correct. Immobility slows peristalsis.
Incorrect. Antibiotics are more likely to cause diarrhea.
Incorrect. Fiber adds bulk and holds water, keeping stool soft.
Correct. Opioids slow the bowel and constipate.
questions.rationale: Several factors affect how fast the bowel runs, including diet, fluid, activity, and medications. Opioids and iron constipate, immobility slows peristalsis, and low fluid intake makes stool harder and drier. This client has four risks at once, so a prevention plan is needed early. Antibiotics are tempting to select because they are a medication that affects the bowel, but they usually cause diarrhea rather than constipation.
questions.takeaway: Opioids, iron, immobility, and low fluid intake all promote constipation.
questions.hintContent: Sort each factor by whether it slows or speeds the bowel.
questions.hintStrategy: For risk-factor SATA, decide the direction of each factor's effect before selecting.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 68-year-old client has frequent liquid stools and reddened perianal skin. Which actions should the nurse take to protect the skin? Select all that apply.
options: Check and change the brief at the end of each shift
Apply a moisture barrier after cleansing
Cleanse the area gently after each stool
Pat the skin dry rather than rubbing
Scrub the skin firmly with soap and water
optionRationales: Incorrect. Prolonged contact with liquid stool worsens skin breakdown.
Correct. A barrier protects the skin from contact with liquid stool.
Correct. Gentle cleansing removes irritating enzymes and acids without causing friction.
Correct. Patting reduces friction on irritated skin.
Incorrect. Firm scrubbing damages irritated skin.
questions.rationale: Liquid stool contains digestive enzymes and acids that irritate the perianal skin, which is why diarrhea carries a risk for skin breakdown. The nurse cleanses gently after each stool, pats the skin dry, and applies a moisture barrier. Scrubbing firmly is tempting because it seems more thorough, but it adds friction to skin that is already damaged. Prompt changes limit the time stool sits against the skin.
questions.takeaway: With diarrhea: cleanse gently after each stool, pat dry, and apply a moisture barrier.
questions.hintContent: Think about what in liquid stool harms the skin and how friction adds to that damage.
questions.hintStrategy: Select actions that reduce both contact time and friction.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client is admitted with diverticulitis. Which findings suggest a complication and should be reported to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: Increasing distention with no stool or flatus
Lower left abdominal pain present on admission
Bright red blood passed rectally
A rigid, board-like abdomen with rising fever
A soft, formed brown stool this morning
optionRationales: Correct. Swelling and scarring can narrow or block the colon, causing obstruction.
Incorrect. Lower left pain is a typical presenting symptom of diverticulitis, not a new complication.
Correct. Bleeding from vessels near the pouches is a complication of diverticulitis.
Correct. This suggests perforation with peritonitis.
Incorrect. A normal stool suggests the bowel is moving.
questions.rationale: Diverticulitis is inflammation of the diverticula, and its three serious complications are obstruction, perforation, and bleeding. Rectal bleeding, a rigid abdomen with fever, and increasing distention without stool or flatus each point to one of these. Lower left abdominal pain is tempting to select because it is abnormal, but it is the usual presenting symptom of diverticulitis, present since admission. The nurse watches for changes that signal one of the three complications.
questions.takeaway: Diverticulitis complications: obstruction, perforation, and bleeding.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three complications of inflamed diverticula and the sign of each.
questions.hintStrategy: In complication SATA, separate the expected presenting symptoms from new findings that signal a complication.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 57-year-old client is admitted with a suspected small bowel obstruction. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
options: An increased appetite
Cramping abdominal pain
No passage of stool or flatus
Abdominal distention
Frequent large, loose stools
Nausea and vomiting
optionRationales: Incorrect. Distention, nausea, and vomiting reduce appetite.
Correct. Stretching of the bowel causes cramping pain.
Correct. Contents cannot move past the obstruction.
Correct. Fluid, gas, and stool build up and stretch the bowel.
Incorrect. An obstruction stops the passage of stool rather than increasing it.
Correct. Contents back up behind the obstruction.
questions.rationale: A bowel obstruction is the inability of intestinal contents to move through the small or large bowel. Fluid, gas, and stool build up behind it, so the bowel stretches and the client develops distention, cramping pain, nausea and vomiting, and stops passing stool and flatus. Frequent loose stools are tempting if you remember that an impaction can cause leakage, but a true obstruction stops the passage of stool. Recognizing the pattern early allows prompt reporting before necrosis or perforation.
questions.takeaway: Bowel obstruction: distention, cramping pain, nausea and vomiting, and no stool or flatus.
questions.hintContent: Picture what builds up behind a blockage and what the client cannot pass.
questions.hintStrategy: For expected-finding SATA, reason from the mechanism: what stops, and what backs up?

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse reviews the records of several clients on a surgical unit. Which factors increase the risk of a paralytic ileus, a functional obstruction? Select all that apply.
options: Scar tissue bands from several past surgeries
General anesthesia for a colon resection yesterday
A colon tumor seen on CT before surgery
Morphine by patient-controlled analgesia
Major abdominal surgery with handling of the bowel
optionRationales: Incorrect. Adhesions cause mechanical obstruction, not a functional one.
Correct. Anesthesia and abdominal surgery can stop intestinal muscle movement.
Incorrect. A tumor causes a mechanical obstruction, a physical block.
Correct. Opioids are drugs that slow or stop peristalsis.
Correct. Paralytic ileus often occurs after surgery.
questions.rationale: A functional obstruction means the bowel is open but peristalsis cannot push contents forward. Paralytic ileus, in which the intestinal muscles become adynamic, often occurs after surgery or drugs such as anesthesia and opioids. Mechanical obstructions, by contrast, involve a physical block such as adhesions, hernias, intussusception, volvulus, or tumors. Adhesions are tempting because they are linked to past surgery, but they block the bowel physically rather than stopping its motor.
questions.takeaway: Paralytic ileus (functional) follows surgery, anesthesia, and opioids; adhesions and tumors cause mechanical obstruction.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each factor stops the bowel's motor or physically blocks the bowel.
questions.hintStrategy: For look-alike categories, sort each option into one category before deciding.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is screening clients in a long-term care facility for risk of fecal incontinence. Which clients are at increased risk? Select all that apply.
options: A resident with advanced dementia
A resident with severe depression
A resident who walks daily and eats high-fiber foods
A resident with a spinal cord injury
A resident who takes iron and has dark, formed stools
optionRationales: Correct. Dementia interferes with recognizing and responding to the urge.
Correct. Depression can reduce motivation or ability to respond to the urge.
Incorrect. Activity and fiber support normal bowel function.
Correct. Spinal cord injury interferes with sensation and sphincter control.
Incorrect. Iron darkens and can harden stool; it does not cause loss of control.
questions.rationale: Bowel control requires sensing that the rectum is full, a strong sphincter to hold stool, and a brain that can respond. Neurologic disorders such as stroke, spinal cord injury, and dementia interfere with sensation or control, and depression can reduce a person's ability to respond to the urge. Fecal incontinence is usually a manifestation of one of these disorders, so the nurse looks for the cause. The resident taking iron is tempting because dark stools look abnormal, but iron causes constipation, not loss of control.
questions.takeaway: Neurologic disorders and depression raise fecal incontinence risk; look for the underlying cause.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three things needed for bowel control and which conditions disrupt them.
questions.hintStrategy: In risk SATA, select clients whose condition affects sensation, sphincter strength, or the ability to respond.
